# Introduction

These exercises use `datasets::Loblolly`, a dataset built into R. It contains
84 tree-height observations: `height` is in feet, `age` is in years, and
`Seed` identifies a tree. There are 14 trees, each measured at six ages. The
[Chapter 7 theory](../Theory.qmd) introduces the grouped-model ideas used here.

Work through the exercises in order. RTMB performs the marginalisation after
you mark effects as random; you do not need to implement Laplace approximation
yourself.

We will use the saturating growth curve, a shifted
[saturating exponential](../../Supplements/deterministic-functions.qmd#sec-fn-monomolecular),

$$
m(t;A,R_0,k)=A-(A-R_0)e^{-kt}, \qquad A>0,\quad k>0.
$$

Here $t$ is age, $R_0$ is the extrapolated height at age zero, $A$ is the
asymptotic height, and $k$ controls the approach to that asymptote. The first
observed age is greater than zero, so interpret $R_0$ as an extrapolation rather
than a directly observed height.

# Exercise 1: Grouping and complete pooling

1. Load `datasets::Loblolly`, make an integer `tree_index` suitable for RTMB,
   and count trees and observations per tree. Identify the observational and
   grouping units.
2. Plot height against age for each tree. Use both line type or symbol and colour
   to distinguish trees.
3. Fit a complete-pooling normal model with the growth curve above. Check the
   convergence code, report $A$, $R_0$, $k$, and
   $\sigma^2_{\mathrm{obs}}$ with their units, and overlay the fitted common
   curve.
4. Describe one systematic feature of the tree trajectories that this common
   curve misses.

## Solution

`Loblolly` is supplied with R, so we can copy it to an object for this analysis.
An observation is one recorded height at one age for one tree. A tree is the
grouping unit. `as.integer()` changes the factor levels to consecutive indices
that can index a parameter vector.

```r
library(RTMB)

trees = datasets::Loblolly
trees$tree_index = as.integer(trees$Seed)
table(trees$tree_index)
c(number_trees = length(unique(trees$tree_index)),
  number_observations = nrow(trees))

tree_colours = rep(c("black", "#0072B2", "#D55E00", "#009E73"),
                    length.out = 14)
tree_symbols = rep(c(16, 17, 15, 18), length.out = 14)
plot(trees$age, trees$height, type = "n",
     xlab = "Age (years)", ylab = "Height (feet)")
for (j in 1:14) {
  tree_data = trees[trees$tree_index == j, ]
  lines(tree_data$age, tree_data$height, lty = (j - 1) %% 4 + 1,
        col = tree_colours[j])
  points(tree_data$age, tree_data$height, pch = tree_symbols[j],
         col = tree_colours[j])
}
```

The normal model describes heights conditional on age as independent around the
common curve. Its `sd` argument is a standard deviation, so we estimate
`sigma_obs` on a log scale and square it to report
$\sigma^2_{\mathrm{obs}}$ in squared feet.

```r
tree_mean = function(age, A, R0, k) {
  A - (A - R0) * exp(-k * age)
}

complete_model = function(par) {
  A = exp(par$log_A)
  k = exp(par$log_k)
  sigma_obs = exp(par$log_sigma_obs)
  mu = tree_mean(trees$age, A = A, R0 = par$R0, k = k)
  trees$height %~% dnorm(mean = mu, sd = sigma_obs)
}

complete_start = list(
  log_A = log(max(trees$height) + 5),
  R0 = min(trees$height),
  log_k = log(0.05),
  log_sigma_obs = log(sd(trees$height))
)
complete_obj = MakeADFun(complete_model, complete_start, silent = TRUE)
complete_fit = optim(par = complete_obj$par, fn = complete_obj$fn,
                     gr = complete_obj$gr, method = "BFGS")
complete_fit$convergence

complete_estimates = c(
  A_feet = exp(complete_fit$par["log_A"]),
  R0_feet = complete_fit$par["R0"],
  k_per_year = exp(complete_fit$par["log_k"]),
  sigma2_obs_squared_feet = exp(complete_fit$par["log_sigma_obs"])^2
)
complete_estimates

age_grid = seq(min(trees$age), max(trees$age), length.out = 200)
lines(age_grid,
      tree_mean(age_grid, A = complete_estimates["A_feet"],
                R0 = complete_estimates["R0_feet"],
                k = complete_estimates["k_per_year"]),
      lwd = 3)
```

You should inspect the code returned by `complete_fit$convergence`; zero is
reassuring but does not verify the model. The common curve misses systematic
between-tree differences: some trajectories lie mainly above it while others
lie below it.

# Exercise 2: No pooling

Keep $R_0$, $k$, and $\sigma^2_{\mathrm{obs}}$ shared, but give every tree a
separate asymptote $A_j$ on the log scale.

1. Fit this model with RTMB and check convergence.
2. Plot the fitted curve for every tree and identify the large differences from
   the complete-pooling curve.
3. State which parameters and data remain shared. Are the 14 log asymptotes
   random effects?


Separate log asymptotes keep all fitted asymptotes positive. They are a vector
of ordinary fitted parameters: do not declare this vector `random`.

```r
no_pool_model = function(par) {
  A = exp(par$log_A_tree[trees$tree_index])
  k = exp(par$log_k)
  sigma_obs = exp(par$log_sigma_obs)
  mu = tree_mean(trees$age, A = A, R0 = par$R0, k = k)
  trees$height %~% dnorm(mean = mu, sd = sigma_obs)
}

no_pool_start = list(
  log_A_tree = rep(log(max(trees$height) + 5), 14),
  R0 = complete_estimates["R0_feet"],
  log_k = log(0.05),
  log_sigma_obs = log(sd(trees$height))
)
no_pool_obj = MakeADFun(no_pool_model, no_pool_start, silent = TRUE)
no_pool_fit = optim(par = no_pool_obj$par, fn = no_pool_obj$fn,
                    gr = no_pool_obj$gr, method = "BFGS")
no_pool_fit$convergence

no_pool_A = exp(no_pool_fit$par[grep("log_A_tree", names(no_pool_fit$par))])
no_pool_A

plot(trees$age, trees$height, type = "n",
     xlab = "Age (years)", ylab = "Height (feet)")
for (j in 1:14) {
  tree_data = trees[trees$tree_index == j, ]
  lines(tree_data$age,
        tree_mean(tree_data$age, A = no_pool_A[j],
                  R0 = no_pool_fit$par["R0"],
                  k = exp(no_pool_fit$par["log_k"])),
        lty = (j - 1) %% 4 + 1, col = tree_colours[j])
  points(tree_data$age, tree_data$height, pch = tree_symbols[j],
         col = tree_colours[j])
}
```

The data for all trees still jointly estimate the shared $R_0$, $k$, and
$\sigma^2_{\mathrm{obs}}$. Each tree's data estimate its own log asymptote.
Those 14 parameters are not random effects because the model gives them no
population distribution and does not integrate them out.



# Exercise 3: Partial pooling and shrinkage

Use a log-asymptote random effect so every tree asymptote remains positive:

$$
\log A_j=\log A+u_j,\qquad
u_j\sim\operatorname{Normal}(0,\sigma^2_{\mathrm{tree}}).
$$

1. Fit this model in RTMB, using `random = "u"`, and inspect convergence.
2. Report $A$, $R_0$, $k$, $\sigma^2_{\mathrm{tree}}$, and
   $\sigma^2_{\mathrm{obs}}$. State that the tree variance is on the
   log-asymptote scale and that the observation variance is in squared feet.
3. Draw conditional tree curves and compare their asymptotes with the no-pooling
   curves. Identify the shrinkage pattern.
4. Explain what RTMB did when `u` was declared random.


The log-asymptote formulation keeps $A_j=\exp(\log A+u_j)$ positive. The
standard deviation `sigma_tree` is on the log-asymptote scale, so its square is
$\sigma^2_{\mathrm{tree}}$ on that scale. `sigma_obs` remains in feet and its
square is in squared feet.

```r
partial_model = function(par) {
  A = exp(par$log_A + par$u[trees$tree_index])
  k = exp(par$log_k)
  sigma_tree = exp(par$log_sigma_tree)
  sigma_obs = exp(par$log_sigma_obs)
  mu = tree_mean(trees$age, A = A, R0 = par$R0, k = k)
  par$u %~% dnorm(mean = 0, sd = sigma_tree)
  trees$height %~% dnorm(mean = mu, sd = sigma_obs)
}

partial_start = list(
  log_A = log(max(trees$height) + 5),
  R0 = complete_estimates["R0_feet"],
  log_k = log(0.05),
  log_sigma_tree = log(0.1),
  log_sigma_obs = log(sd(trees$height)),
  u = rep(0, 14)
)
partial_obj = MakeADFun(partial_model, partial_start,
                         random = "u", silent = TRUE)
partial_fit = optim(par = partial_obj$par, fn = partial_obj$fn,
                    gr = partial_obj$gr, method = "BFGS")
partial_fit$convergence

partial_estimates = c(
  A_feet = exp(partial_fit$par["log_A"]),
  R0_feet = partial_fit$par["R0"],
  k_per_year = exp(partial_fit$par["log_k"]),
  sigma2_tree_log_asymptote = exp(partial_fit$par["log_sigma_tree"])^2,
  sigma2_obs_squared_feet = exp(partial_fit$par["log_sigma_obs"])^2
)
partial_estimates

conditional_parameters = partial_obj$env$parList(
  partial_obj$env$last.par.best
)
conditional_u = conditional_parameters$u
partial_A = exp(partial_fit$par["log_A"] + conditional_u)

plot(trees$age, trees$height, type = "n",
     xlab = "Age (years)", ylab = "Height (feet)")
for (j in 1:14) {
  tree_data = trees[trees$tree_index == j, ]
  lines(tree_data$age,
        tree_mean(tree_data$age, A = partial_A[j],
                  R0 = partial_fit$par["R0"],
                  k = exp(partial_fit$par["log_k"])),
        lty = (j - 1) %% 4 + 1, col = tree_colours[j])
  points(tree_data$age, tree_data$height, pch = tree_symbols[j],
         col = tree_colours[j])
}
data.frame(no_pooling = no_pool_A, partial_pooling = partial_A)
```

The conditional effects are used here to draw and compare curves. They should
usually be closer to the common asymptote than the no-pooling estimates: that
is shrinkage. RTMB integrated the unobserved `u` values out of the objective
with Laplace approximation before `optim()` fitted the shared parameters.


# Exercise 4: Interpretation and checking

1. Use the Hessian from the partial-pooling fit to calculate an approximate 95%
   interval for the common asymptote $A$ on the feet scale. State the relevant
   assumptions.
2. Explain the difference between a fitted curve for an observed tree and a
   prediction for a new tree.
3. Simulate complete hierarchical data from the partial-pooling fit: simulate
   one tree effect per tree and then one observation per recorded age. Plot the
   simulated and observed trajectories for comparison.
4. Give at least two limitations of this analysis, including the 14 groups and
   the decision to vary only one curve component.

## Solution

The Hessian is on the fitted parameter scale. We first make its dimensions
explicit, then form an interval for `log_A` and exponentiate its endpoints to
return to feet. This is a quadratic, large-sample approximation and is
especially uncertain if the Hessian is not invertible, the fit has not
converged, or the group variance is near its boundary.

```r
partial_hessian = partial_obj$he(partial_fit$par)
dimnames(partial_hessian) = list(names(partial_fit$par),
                                 names(partial_fit$par))
partial_covariance = solve(partial_hessian)
se_log_A = sqrt(partial_covariance["log_A", "log_A"])
A_interval_feet = exp(
  partial_fit$par["log_A"] +
    c(-1, 1) * qnorm(p = 0.975) * se_log_A
)
A_interval_feet
```

A fitted curve for an observed tree conditions on that tree's estimated
deviation. A prediction for a new tree must also allow for a new draw from the
among-tree distribution, so it includes both tree-level and observation-level
variation.

The simulation below retains the observed ages and grouping structure. It first
draws 14 new tree deviations, then generates height measurements around each
tree's curve. Simulating observation variation alone would fail to check the
grouped model.

```r
set.seed(seed = 801)
sigma_tree = exp(partial_fit$par["log_sigma_tree"])
sigma_obs = exp(partial_fit$par["log_sigma_obs"])
simulated_u = rnorm(n = 14, mean = 0, sd = sigma_tree)
simulated_A = exp(partial_fit$par["log_A"] + simulated_u)
simulated_mu = tree_mean(
  trees$age,
  A = simulated_A[trees$tree_index],
  R0 = partial_fit$par["R0"],
  k = exp(partial_fit$par["log_k"])
)
simulated_height = rnorm(n = nrow(trees), mean = simulated_mu,
                         sd = sigma_obs)

old_par = par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(trees$age, trees$height, type = "n",
     xlab = "Age (years)", ylab = "Observed height (feet)")
plot(trees$age, simulated_height, type = "n",
     xlab = "Age (years)", ylab = "Simulated height (feet)")
for (j in 1:14) {
  tree_data = trees$tree_index == j
  lines(trees$age[tree_data], trees$height[tree_data],
        lty = (j - 1) %% 4 + 1, col = tree_colours[j])
  lines(trees$age[tree_data], simulated_height[tree_data],
        lty = (j - 1) %% 4 + 1, col = tree_colours[j])
}
par(old_par)
```

Compare the range, spacing, and shapes of complete trajectories, not just the
pointwise scatter. This model has only 14 groups, assumes normally distributed
log-asymptote deviations, and allows trees to differ only in asymptote. It may
miss differences in initial height, rate of approach, dependence across ages,
or an unsuitable normal observation distribution.
